speaker_role: independent educational consultant (Amy Goforth, Goforth Admissions Consulting)
commercial_incentive: yes - runs her own admissions consulting business (Goforth Admissions Consulting)
key_insights: Early decision (ED) is binding and tends to favor universities' yield rate and revenue since ED admits are disproportionately full-pay, since there's little incentive to offer merit aid to students already committed
Early action (EA) is non-binding and signals interest, but many EA applicants end up deferred to the regular round rather than getting an early yes/no

Restrictive early action (used by schools like Stanford, Harvard, Princeton) is non-binding but bars applying early to other private schools; the speaker says Stanford gives clear yes/no answers rather than mass deferrals
Early decision two (ED2) is a later-cycle binding option, useful for students denied or deferred elsewhere who pivot to a new binding first choice

The speaker states ED can raise admission odds meaningfully (she cites an example of roughly 8% regular vs 12% ED at one prestigious school, and up to a 20% advantage at some other schools), while restrictive early action gives only a slight edge even at Stanford
specific_numbers_or_facts: Early action deadlines are commonly November 1st, per the speaker; University of Tennessee and University of Georgia deadlines cited as around October 15
Common App opens August 1st, per the speaker
Example admission-rate advantage cited by the speaker: ~8% regular decision vs ~12% early decision at one prestigious school, with some schools showing up to a 20% ED advantage
Anecdote: two of the speaker's Stanford restrictive-early-action applicants, one admitted and one denied outright (not deferred), with the denied student later admitted via a different school's ED2
notable_or_distinctive: Frames the historical origin of these admission plans (regular decision, then ED in the 1950s-60s at Harvard and peers, then EA about a decade later as an equity response, then restrictive EA and ED2) rather than just defining the terms.
reliability_notes: Admission-rate figures and the historical timeline are presented without citations and appear to be the consultant's own general knowledge/experience rather than sourced data; the client anecdotes are single, unverified cases.
